question: What concerns did customers raise about pricing?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every concern, objection, complaint or question the customer raises about pricing, cost, budget, discounts, fees, contract value or return on investment, quoting the customer's words where possible and noting whether the concern was resolved, deferred or left open.
assumptions: No call type restriction because the question asks about customers in general.
Concerns are interpreted to include objections, complaints and questions about cost or value.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison, but that's the number that was in my head.
findings.context: Customer says Growth pricing ($1,800/month) is more than expected, anchored on Zapier as a benchmark, which they admit is not a fair comparison. — Deferred: OrbitFlow said it would return to pricing once the user model is known (T041), so the concern is not resolved on this call.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
findings.context: Customer can justify the price only if the platform replaces enough manual work and some Gainsight spend, and needs a clearer ROI story than time savings. — Open: OrbitFlow proposed baselining elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate and engineer hours for a pilot (T142), but no ROI case was agreed on the call.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true.
findings.context: Customer will not sell the business case internally as headcount reduction, because it would not survive the CFO and is not true; the stronger case is consistency and speed. — Shapes the ROI framing rather than objecting to price directly. OrbitFlow had asked which ROI lens applied (T139).

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And there's an engineering cost nobody sees. A script takes two days to write and then quietly eats a few hours every month forever. That never makes it into the original estimate.
findings.context: Customer says hidden ongoing engineering maintenance cost of scripts is never in the original estimate. — Customer-raised cost concern about total cost of ownership of the current approach. OrbitFlow proposed baselining engineer hours spent maintaining the current process (T142).

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Please make that explicit in the proposal. I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Customer does not want to discover mid-contract that occasional approvers need full paid seats; wants seat requirements explicit in the proposal. — Open pricing-model concern. OrbitFlow agreed to itemise builder and viewer/approver counts but did not give a number (T135, T137).

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: Yes, because we may have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or receive a notification.
findings.context: Customer's team may have few builders but many approval-only or notification-only users, so per-seat cost depends on how users are categorised. — Deferred: OrbitFlow said approval-only users can be structured differently by package but gave no figures.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor. That's the conversation I'll have to win internally.
findings.context: Customer says the real commercial question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract rather than add another vendor, and this is the internal battle they must win. — Open: OrbitFlow agreed to write it as a pilot exit criterion (T129). Tom also named Workato or improving the status quo as the honest comparison (T153).

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
findings.context: Customer requires a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises as a condition for moving from evaluation to decision. — Stated decision criterion; not resolved on the call.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year, so — yes, finance gets involved.
findings.context: Purchases above $25,000 a year trigger finance involvement at the customer. — Budget-approval threshold stated by customer, relevant to deal size and approval path.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Honestly? I'm not ready to react to that.
findings.context: Customer is not ready to react to OrbitFlow's Enterprise pricing and defers any pricing conversation until the BAA question is answered. Status: deferred, not resolved. — Maya quoted Growth from $1,800/month for up to 30 users on annual terms and said Enterprise is custom-priced. Priya deferred. Maya agreed not to push, and the price discussion is tied to the security/BAA gate.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met.
findings.context: Procurement will not hold a serious pricing conversation until security confirms the BAA requirement can be met. If the answer is no, price is irrelevant. — Deferral of pricing to the security gate. Priya said this was not a negotiating position. Status: deferred.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: What counts as a user?
findings.context: Customer asks what counts as a licensed user, since they expect a few builders and many occasional approvers or notification recipients. — Raised as a pricing-model question. Maya said builders and full workspace users are licensed, and approval-only or notification-only users may be structured differently. Maya declined to quote a figure until the user model is known. Status: open.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Customer does not want to discover later that every occasional approver needs a full seat, and wants the seat model explicit in the proposal. — Cost-surprise concern. Maya committed to an itemised proposal covering assumed builders, viewers, approvers, expected volume and one-time services. Status: deferred to the proposal, with a commitment from the vendor.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
findings.context: Customer wants a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises as a condition for a decision. — Stated among criteria for moving from evaluation to a decision. Status: open.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: eleven weeks of waiting has a number attached to it somewhere.
findings.context: Customer's ROI case rests on consistency and speed rather than headcount, and the backlog has a real cost even though it is hard to quantify. — Value/ROI framing. Priya rejected a headcount-based case. Maya proposed baselining elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate, or systems-group hours. Priya said the systems-group hours measure is the one her director cares about.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
findings.context: Power Automate is already covered by the customer's Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement, so an alternative that replaces it on cost grounds is a real comparison. — Licensing/cost context from the customer. Maya said a proposal to migrate everything off Microsoft would lose to the licensing agreement, and Priya agreed.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
findings.context: Sophie Reed said Growth's £/$1,800 per month price is hard for a team their size; she had expected roughly 800-1,000 per month, and the gap is left open. — Core pricing objection. Vendor acknowledged the gap but did not close it. Left open.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I could potentially do an annual prepay if that materially changes the number. Does it?
findings.context: Sophie Reed asked whether an annual prepay would materially change the price; Leo said it gives a meaningful discount but not a halving. Deferred/left open. — Customer probed discount options; vendor said discount is modest.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: the two hundred doesn't include the four hours a week you spend chasing broken ones.
findings.context: Sophie Reed said the current Zapier spend (about 200-something) understates the real cost, because it excludes roughly four hours a week of chasing broken automations; Marcus said it is more than four hours. Customer frames ROI in terms of hidden labour cost. — Customer argument that total cost of current setup is higher than the licence bill. Left open; Marcus later agreed to log time.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: I genuinely don't know. Nobody's ever asked me to count it.
findings.context: Marcus Lee said nobody has asked him to count the cost of the current broken-automation time, so the ROI is unknown. Deferred to a four-week logging exercise. — Business case gap; customer cannot yet quantify value. Deferred.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
findings.context: Sophie Reed said budget is the biggest risk and that the team may decide it is over-buying and keep Zapier; she also said she can approve tools under 15,000 a year alone, and the Growth price (21,600 a year) goes to the COO and finance director. — Approval threshold and budget risk. Left open; slower process above threshold.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Sophie Reed said she likes the monitoring and templates but is not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools they already pay for. Left open. — Final stance on value versus cost. Customer is not saying no.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
findings.context: Sophie Reed asked whether the AI features or usage-based pricing would cost extra; Leo said usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connectors and would be modelled. Customer is wary of surprise costs. Deferred. — Hidden-fee concern about usage pricing.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review.
findings.context: Customer says the headline licence price will not surprise him, but he cares about transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and costs only discovered after architecture review; deferred to proposal transparency commitment. — Pricing concern raised by customer; vendor committed to itemised proposal, so partially addressed but open until the proposal arrives.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: The proposal will separate licence, assumed builder count, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, and services as distinct line items, with the assumptions written next to each.
findings.context: Customer asks vendor to separate licence, builder count, viewer/approver population, workflow volume and services; vendor committed to itemised line items with assumptions, and 'to be determined' where unknown. — Vendor response to pricing transparency concern; resolved as a commitment, to be verified in the written proposal.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: We may have twenty people building and several hundred who only approve something.
findings.context: Customer wants explicit pricing for occasional approvers and fears paying full seats for them in year two; vendor said it would be explicit but gave no number. — Seat cost concern; deferred pending user model and architecture review.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Please put that in the proposal explicitly. I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
findings.context: Customer does not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver needs a full seat. — Explicit concern about per-seat cost scaling; vendor committed to make it explicit.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: a script takes two days to write and then consumes a few hours every month forever. That never appears in the original estimate.
findings.context: Customer says the case is cycle time and error reduction, not headcount, and that an unbudgeted ongoing maintenance cost of scripts is a hidden cost not in original estimates; ROI concern. — ROI framing; customer notes maintenance cost is never counted.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: I don't have a number, but it is meaningful.
findings.context: Customer says the savings from catching the SAP/Salesforce mismatch at contract close is meaningful but unquantified; he will not give an invented number. ROI left open. — Value of phase-one use case unquantified; deferred to baseline.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Not headcount. I want to be very clear about that because in a manufacturing business the word automation makes people nervous for reasons that have nothing to do with software.
findings.context: Customer says a manufacturing business does not want automation framed as headcount reduction. — ROI framing constraint; the customer explicitly rules out headcount savings as a justification.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Thank you. That is exactly the thing I was going to raise later.
findings.context: Vendor says professional services for SAP/on-prem work may be significant and will be priced up front; customer welcomes this as a previously unraised concern. — Services cost concern raised by vendor and welcomed by customer; open until architecture review.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Usage overages. If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine.
findings.context: Customer raised concern about unpredictable usage overage charges growing the bill over time; vendor deferred specifics until modelling volumes, with overage mechanism to be put explicitly in contract (left open pending modelling). — Noah raised the pricing concern about second-year invoices; vendor committed to modelling and contract terms but gave no specific cap. Open.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Can you cap it?
findings.context: Customer asked whether usage could be capped; vendor declined to promise a cap before modelling volumes. Left open. — Direct pricing question about a cap; vendor avoided committing on the call.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: The range is roughly where I expected an enterprise workflow product to land. That's not my concern.
findings.context: Customer said the overall price range was roughly where expected for enterprise, so base price was not a concern; the concern was usage overages. — Customer explicitly deprioritised base price; resolved for base price on the call.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Make that split explicit in the proposal. I don't want to find out in year two that every approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Customer wants per-user licensing split explicit so approver-only users do not require full seats; concern about year-two cost. — Licensing concern about seat counts for 40 builders and up to 300 approvers/viewers; vendor agreed to itemise. Deferred to proposal.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Three hundred is optimistic, by the way. It might be more.
findings.context: Customer noted user count may grow beyond 300, raising cost exposure; vendor agreed to model 300 and 500 users. — Seat-count growth concern; vendor to model scenarios. Deferred.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Not headcount. I want to be clear about that — I'm not going to sell this as a reduction
findings.context: Customer said the business case is consistency, auditability and key-person dependency, not headcount reduction; ROI framed around audit remediation budget. — ROI discussion; customer explicitly not claiming cost savings. Resolved as a framing.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
findings.context: Customer said the Growth package price of eighteen hundred a month was above what she had in mind. — Initial price reaction to Growth package; left open, no resolution on price in the call.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Is there any way to start with ten users? Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
findings.context: Customer asked whether she could start with ten users or bill monthly to prove the process before committing to an annual contract. — Customer sought lower-commitment pricing; vendor said monthly was 'usually fine' but needed manager approval, so left open and deferred.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
findings.context: Customer objected to paying for thirty seats when she needed ten, saying she would be paying for twenty seats she does not need. — Seat-count objection; vendor said the thirty-user package price is fixed. Not resolved.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
findings.context: Customer stated her spending authority is capped at twenty thousand; anything above requires founder approval, and the proposed annual cost exceeds that. — Budget constraint; Ben computed the annual figure as twenty-one and a half thousand. Left open.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: he'll ask what we get for twenty-one thousand that we don't get from Zapier for two thousand, and I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
findings.context: Customer questioned the return on investment versus Zapier, asking what the company gets for twenty-one thousand that it does not get from Zapier for two thousand. — ROI/value concern raised for founder approval; vendor answered with governance and audit trail, which customer rejected as irrelevant to an agency. Left open.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Price and complexity are the two risks. And honestly, we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough
findings.context: Customer said Zapier plus better process discipline may be good enough, so price and complexity are real risks to the deal. — Price-driven alternative; customer said she is interested but not dismissing it. Open.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: can you confirm the monthly billing thing properly rather than "probably"? Because if that's not actually available I'd rather know now.
findings.context: Customer wants vendor to confirm monthly billing explicitly, saying she would rather know now if it is unavailable. — Pricing term not confirmed; vendor said he would check with his manager. Deferred.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Because that's actually the question. Not whether they signed.
findings.context: Customer said the vendor's ROI argument about lost clients did not answer her cost concern, and that the reference should show the onboarding problem was fixed, not just that the client signed. — Customer pushed back on the vendor's anecdote about a lost client justifying price; deferred pending reference.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The price might be defensible for central operations. What I need to understand is the licensing model.
findings.context: Customer says the price may be defensible for central operations, but the real question is the licensing model; the concern is left open. — Carlos raises pricing after vendor gives Growth and Enterprise headline figures. Not resolved; vendor deferred a number.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
findings.context: Customer objects that supervisors would need full seats, which would make the deal unviable; concern left open pending a builder vs approver breakdown. — Licensing model concern. Vendor said approval-only populations can be structured differently, but gave no number.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Six builders, several hundred approvers.
findings.context: Customer states the population sizes: about six builders and several hundred approvers, which bears on licensing cost. — Customer supplied the counts so vendor could structure pricing; vendor said the shape must be explicit in writing before any internal take-forward.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
findings.context: Customer says Power Automate's favourable licensing matters, and that the comparison is partly about cost. Vendor conceded it cannot beat bundled licensing on price; the customer's internal case must be operational cost rather than licence cost. — Cost comparison against incumbent. Deferred to operational-cost argument; the customer's own internal case is still to be built.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: That's the argument I'd have to make internally, yes.
findings.context: Customer accepts that the case must rest on operational cost; the time spent debugging flows is unmeasured, and the customer's estimate of a day a week was a guess. — ROI framing. Vendor asked for a measurement; customer agreed to measure for a month. Left open. Lucy's figure was explicitly marked as a guess.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
findings.context: Customer says the economic case for OrbitFlow must be material, since it would require working around embedded Power Automate. — Value bar set by customer. Left open; tests proposed but not run.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: We end up spending a great deal to automate something that saves a business services person four hours a week.
findings.context: Samir Khan says the integration effort may be disproportionate to the value, since automating the process saves only about four hours a week of business services time. This is his stated biggest risk and is left open pending the integration assessment and services estimate. — Customer ROI concern about cost versus value. Vendor (Leo Grant) responded that the test is an operation-by-operation difficulty assessment plus a services estimate, to be compared against the cost of delayed matter opening. Left open.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Do we have a number for what it costs?
findings.context: Eleanor Brooks asks whether there is a cost figure for matter-opening delay, and admits there is none. Without that number the business case cannot be quantified. — Return-on-investment gap. Leo Grant suggested client-facing cost of delay as the number; Eleanor agreed it was a good reframe. Left open, with a follow-up to get the number.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: It's also harder to evidence.
findings.context: Samir Khan says the value of the automation is hard to evidence. — Follows the discussion of client-relationship cost of delay. Left open; Eleanor agreed everything worth measuring is harder to evidence.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: The enterprise range itself doesn't worry me. We buy expensive software.
findings.context: Eleanor Brooks says the Enterprise price range is not a concern, but the scope of value is. She will not make a business case that depends on privileged-content use, and she would be less interested if it were upsold. — Price tier is accepted, but the business case must stay within low-risk operational scope. Vendor agreed to scope the proposal that way. Resolved for the Enterprise tier; the privileged-content upsell is ruled out.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: What's a user? We'd have very few builders and a very large number of partners who approve something occasionally.
findings.context: Samir Khan asks how a user is defined, expecting few builders but many partners who approve only occasionally, which affects licence cost. — Per-seat licensing question. Vendor declined to give a number until the licensed-user split is known, saying a number would be misleading. Deferred.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Please put the split in writing when you do. If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
findings.context: Eleanor Brooks asks for the seat split in writing, warning that if every partner needs a seat the deal becomes a very short conversation. — Seat-cost sensitivity. Vendor committed to providing the split in writing. Deferred pending that document.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: The spend is very questionable. But that's a separate fight.
findings.context: Customer questioned the value of the existing Gainsight spend and called it questionable, while noting it is a separate fight from the OrbitFlow decision. — Cost concern about existing spend, raised when discussing consolidation; Darren says it is separate and Maya declines to get in the middle, so it is left open.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I think the price is reasonable if it lets us consolidate several manual programmes.
findings.context: Olivia Grant says the price is reasonable only if OrbitFlow lets Inkwell consolidate several manual programmes, including a chunk of Gainsight spend. — Conditional acceptance of price tied to ROI through consolidation; not resolved, since no figure was given.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: A cost model comparing this with expanding Gainsight. Including the implementation effort on both sides
findings.context: Customer wants a cost model comparing OrbitFlow with expanding Gainsight, including implementation effort on both sides, and wants it to be honest even if Gainsight is cheaper. — Customer cost-comparison request; Maya agreed to deliver it in the written follow-up, so it is deferred.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: It relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
findings.context: Customer challenged the ROI case, saying renewal-retention benefit depends on a counterfactual that cannot be proven. — ROI objection; Maya responded by proposing a leading indicator (time from first signal to first intervention), which Darren found a better framing. Partly resolved, but the renewal ROI claim remains unproven.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I don't want to find out in month four that all sixty-two need full seats.
findings.context: Customer wants pricing made explicit by user split so seat costs are not a surprise later, for builders versus the roughly sixty-two task-receiving CSMs. — Concern about per-seat licensing exposure; Maya deferred any figure until the itemised proposal, so it is deferred.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: the forty-percent thing wasn't a licensing failure, it was an implementation failure.
findings.context: Customer said the Gainsight under-implementation was an implementation failure, not a licensing failure, so cost comparisons must count implementation effort. — Relates to cost assumptions behind the Gainsight comparison; raised as a cost-model requirement.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
findings.context: Customer (Ava Sinclair) raised concern that per-event pricing would make high-volume event processing too expensive; left open pending vendor confirmation of pricing unit. — Cost concern about paying per event; vendor said filter upstream so only business events reach OrbitFlow. Customer's concern not fully resolved, she still asked about the pricing unit.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: My question is whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping the event-handling layer in AWS.
findings.context: Customer (Marcus Chen) asked whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic versus keeping the event layer in AWS; he suggested it may answer itself. — Economics question about usage limits; partly answered by vendor saying it depends on what counts as a run; left open.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: If I emit a business event and it triggers a workflow that fans out to five subflows, is that one run or six?
findings.context: Customer (Ava Sinclair) worried that subflow invocations may each be billed as separate runs, which would make the recommended composition pattern expensive; deferred to written billing answer. — Vendor (Nina Patel) said subflow invocations are believed to be counted but could not confirm billing semantics; deferred to written answer due by Friday.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: That's what happened with our observability vendor.
findings.context: Customer (Marcus Chen) said the prior observability vendor's pricing had caused cost problems twice; the bill was a trigger for dropping the tool. — Background on past vendor cost experience shaping the buyer's sensitivity to usage-based invoices.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: I'd like the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, not after. If the economics don't work I'd rather know in week three.
findings.context: Customer (Marcus Chen) asked for the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, so economics can be known by week three; vendor committed to week two. — Commercial concern about ROI/economics; resolved as a commitment, to be delivered in week two.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I think most of what you do could be built internally. We have the skills. The question is whether we should.
findings.context: Customer (Ava Sinclair) said she thinks most of the product could be built internally, questioning whether the platform's cost is justified; deferred to a four-week time-cost test. — Build-versus-buy value concern; the cost argument rests on maintenance time, not license price. Left open pending evaluation.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Were we charged for those?
findings.context: Customer asked whether they were charged for the overage runs, and the vendor said two of the four overage months were charged and two were waived. — Overage billing question; resolved by vendor in the same turn sequence (March waived for retry storm, May waived as a goodwill judgement call).

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
findings.context: Customer said the run tier is wrong because of the overages, which the vendor agreed with. — Run-tier sizing concern raised after overage discussion; vendor said the tier change is the main thing to discuss, so this was deferred to the renewal proposal.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: You're offering to reduce our seat count?
findings.context: Customer questioned the seat reduction, asking whether the vendor was offering to lower their seat count, which implies a cost-reduction question about licences. — Licence/seat count question raised in the adoption discussion; vendor proposed seven seats instead of nine, which the customer then welcomed.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Braced for "here's a fifteen percent uplift, sign here."
findings.context: Customer said she had expected a fifteen percent price uplift at renewal and was braced for it. — Pre-emptive uplift objection; vendor said there is an uplift and would come to it.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: That's more reasonable than I expected.
findings.context: After hearing the standard uplift is seven percent, customer said it was more reasonable than expected. — Uplift concern largely resolved in the call; the vendor still flagged that the run tier increase is a bigger number.

findings.speaker: Devan Shah
findings.quote: What's the delta between three fifty and four hundred?
findings.context: Customer asked for the price gap between the three-hundred-fifty and four-hundred-thousand run tiers, and the vendor deferred exact numbers. — Tier pricing question; vendor said exact numbers would follow, so this was deferred.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Nine percent for forty percent more capacity and a new use case.
findings.context: Customer questioned whether the total spend is justified: nine percent more cost for forty percent more capacity plus a new use case. — Value/ROI concern about the renewal total; vendor said the seat reduction is real and not offset by an inflated run tier. Left open pending the proposal.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: I have to take it to a finance director who will ask what changed and why.
findings.context: Customer asked for the two changes (seat reduction and run-tier increase) shown separately because a finance director will ask what changed and why. — Budget justification requirement; vendor agreed to show last year's and next year's line items side by side. Deferred to the Friday proposal.

findings.speaker: Graham Attwood
findings.quote: That's precisely the position I'm in.
findings.context: Customer says the product is 'a very expensive product that nobody operates' when only one builder is active; Graham agrees he is in that position. — Cost/value concern raised by vendor's hypothetical, accepted by customer; left open (not resolved, tied to enablement plan).

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Is Enterprise worth it for what you're getting', and right now the honest answer is probably not, because you're getting very little.
findings.context: Customer questions whether Enterprise tier is worth the cost given minimal usage of its features; vendor agrees it probably is not. — Return-on-investment concern on tier spend; vendor proposed Growth tier, customer's security requirement (SSO) makes Growth unviable, so left open with a six-month option proposed.

findings.speaker: Graham Attwood
findings.quote: that we're paying for Enterprise and getting very little
findings.context: Customer states they are paying for Enterprise while getting very little value from it. — Customer agrees with the vendor's ROI view; deferred to the renewal decision.

findings.speaker: Graham Attwood
findings.quote: Would you discount six months?

draft.answer: Customers raised several pricing concerns across prospect, renewal, churn and cold calls. The most common were that the headline price (Growth at $1,800/month) was above expectations or unaffordable, and fear of paying full seats for occasional approvers [C1][C2]. Others were hidden or usage-based charges, ROI and value justification versus cheaper alternatives, and approval-threshold and budget constraints [C3][C4][C5]. Churned customers cited paying for unused capacity and no smaller tier [C6]. Some customers said base price was not the concern [C7].

claims.text: Several prospects said Growth at $1,800/month was too high or above expectations: Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan, benchmarked against Zapier), Cedar & Finch (Sophie Reed expected about 800-1,000), and Fable Media (Imogen Price, 'above what I had in mind'). Trafford Dental Group's Yvonne Deeks called it 'not a number that exists in my world', named £200-300/month as her budget, and said price would have meant a no regardless of pitch (one finding on the decisive outcome is inferred).

Per-seat licensing for occasional approvers was a recurring concern. Acme Logistics, BrightPath Health, DeltaWorks Manufacturing (Anika Bose), Ember Financial (Noah Williams, plus Hannah Cole saying users may exceed 300), Greenline Energy Services (Carlos Mendes: 'over before it starts'), Harbor Legal (Samir Khan and Eleanor Brooks) and Inkwell Learning (Olivia Grant, 62 CSMs) did not want to find out later that approvers need full seats. Fable Media's Imogen Price objected to paying for 30 seats when she needed 10. Vendors generally agreed to itemise in the proposal but gave no numbers.

Customers worried about hidden, usage-based or scaling costs. Ember Financial's Noah Williams raised overage unpredictability and asked 'Can you cap it?' (vendor declined to promise a cap). Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed was wary of surprise costs from AI or usage pricing. DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel wanted transparency on services and premium connectors. Acme and BrightPath required a model without hidden scaling surprises. Juniper Cloud Tools' Ava Sinclair and Marcus Chen worried about per-event or per-run billing, and Marcus asked for the pricing model in writing (vendor committed to week two). Lumen Retail's Fiona Bright said the run tier was wrong after overages, and asked for changes shown separately for her finance director.

Customers questioned ROI and value versus cheaper alternatives. Fable Media's Imogen Price asked what $21k buys over Zapier at $2k, and said Zapier plus process discipline may suffice. Acme Logistics wanted a clearer ROI story and was weighing a Workato expansion. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed was not convinced value closes the gap. Greenline said Power Automate's favourable licensing matters. BrightPath cited its Microsoft agreement covering Power Automate. Harbor Legal's Samir Khan feared disproportionate integration spend. Inkwell Learning challenged the retention ROI, and Lumen's Fiona Bright questioned 9% more cost for 40% more capacity. Pinewood Insurance's Graham Attwood said they pay for Enterprise and get very little.

Budget approval thresholds created friction: Acme's finance gets involved above $25k/year, Fable Media's Imogen Price can sign up to £20k (the proposal is about £21.5k), and Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed can approve under 15,000 while Growth (21,600/year) goes to the COO and finance director. Fable Media also asked for monthly billing or starting with 10 users, which was left to manager approval. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed asked about annual prepay, and the vendor said the discount is meaningful but not a halving. Pinewood's Graham Attwood asked about a six-month discount, and the vendor said no discount, only pro-rata.

Churned customers cited poor value for money. Oakhill Property's Hazel Wren said they paid £1,800/month for 30 users with 4 logging in, that £19k was not worth it, and that Zapier at about £2,000/year was cheaper. She refused a discount, and said a plan at £500-600/month would have kept them (with approval forms), but no smaller plan exists. Verity Payments' Kwame Boateng and Sarah Lindqvist said the premium was not worth it and the licence cost went unjustified (about $100k/year). Kwame said Workato was only somewhat cheaper, so price was partly but not primarily the reason for switching.

Some customers said price itself was not the issue: Ember Financial's Noah Williams said the range was as expected, DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel said the headline price would not surprise him, and Harbor Legal's Eleanor Brooks said the Enterprise range does not worry her. Halberd Security's Grace Okonkwo accepted the 7% renewal uplift. Lumen's Fiona Bright had braced for a 15% uplift and found 7% more reasonable.

conflicts.description: Kwame Boateng said price was only partly, not primarily, the reason and Workato was only slightly cheaper, yet Sarah Lindqvist and Kwame also framed the licence cost as unjustified relative to value.

evidence.quote: But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
evidence.context: Customer said the run tier is wrong because of the overages, which the vendor agreed with. — Run-tier sizing concern raised after overage discussion; vendor said the tier change is the main thing to discuss, so this was deferred to the renewal proposal.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: I have to take it to a finance director who will ask what changed and why.
evidence.context: Customer asked for the two changes (seat reduction and run-tier increase) shown separately because a finance director will ask what changed and why. — Budget justification requirement; vendor agreed to show last year's and next year's line items side by side. Deferred to the Friday proposal.

claims.text: Customers questioned ROI and value versus cheaper alternatives. Fable Media's Imogen Price asked what $21k buys over Zapier at $2k, and said Zapier plus process discipline may suffice. Acme Logistics wanted a clearer ROI story and was weighing a Workato expansion. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed was not convinced value closes the gap. Greenline said Power Automate's favourable licensing matters. BrightPath cited its Microsoft agreement covering Power Automate. Harbor Legal's Samir Khan feared disproportionate integration spend. Inkwell Learning challenged the retention ROI, and Lumen's Fiona Bright questioned 9% more cost for 40% more capacity. Pinewood Insurance's Graham Attwood said they pay for Enterprise and get very little.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: he'll ask what we get for twenty-one thousand that we don't get from Zapier for two thousand, and I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
evidence.context: Customer questioned the return on investment versus Zapier, asking what the company gets for twenty-one thousand that it does not get from Zapier for two thousand. — ROI/value concern raised for founder approval; vendor answered with governance and audit trail, which customer rejected as irrelevant to an agency. Left open.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Price and complexity are the two risks. And honestly, we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough
evidence.context: Customer said Zapier plus better process discipline may be good enough, so price and complexity are real risks to the deal. — Price-driven alternative; customer said she is interested but not dismissing it. Open.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
evidence.context: Customer can justify the price only if the platform replaces enough manual work and some Gainsight spend, and needs a clearer ROI story than time savings. — Open: OrbitFlow proposed baselining elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate and engineer hours for a pilot (T142), but no ROI case was agreed on the call.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor. That's the conversation I'll have to win internally.
evidence.context: Customer says the real commercial question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract rather than add another vendor, and this is the internal battle they must win. — Open: OrbitFlow agreed to write it as a pilot exit criterion (T129). Tom also named Workato or improving the status quo as the honest comparison (T153).

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
evidence.context: Sophie Reed said she likes the monitoring and templates but is not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools they already pay for. Left open. — Final stance on value versus cost. Customer is not saying no.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
evidence.context: Customer says Power Automate's favourable licensing matters, and that the comparison is partly about cost. Vendor conceded it cannot beat bundled licensing on price; the customer's internal case must be operational cost rather than licence cost. — Cost comparison against incumbent. Deferred to operational-cost argument; the customer's own internal case is still to be built.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
evidence.context: Power Automate is already covered by the customer's Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement, so an alternative that replaces it on cost grounds is a real comparison. — Licensing/cost context from the customer. Maya said a proposal to migrate everything off Microsoft would lose to the licensing agreement, and Priya agreed.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: We end up spending a great deal to automate something that saves a business services person four hours a week.
evidence.context: Samir Khan says the integration effort may be disproportionate to the value, since automating the process saves only about four hours a week of business services time. This is his stated biggest risk and is left open pending the integration assessment and services estimate. — Customer ROI concern about cost versus value. Vendor (Leo Grant) responded that the test is an operation-by-operation difficulty assessment plus a services estimate, to be compared against the cost of delayed matter opening. Left open.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: It relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
evidence.context: Customer challenged the ROI case, saying renewal-retention benefit depends on a counterfactual that cannot be proven. — ROI objection; Maya responded by proposing a leading indicator (time from first signal to first intervention), which Darren found a better framing. Partly resolved, but the renewal ROI claim remains unproven.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Nine percent for forty percent more capacity and a new use case.
evidence.context: Customer questioned whether the total spend is justified: nine percent more cost for forty percent more capacity plus a new use case. — Value/ROI concern about the renewal total; vendor said the seat reduction is real and not offset by an inflated run tier. Left open pending the proposal.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: that we're paying for Enterprise and getting very little
evidence.context: Customer states they are paying for Enterprise while getting very little value from it. — Customer agrees with the vendor's ROI view; deferred to the renewal decision.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: That's precisely the position I'm in.
evidence.context: Customer says the product is 'a very expensive product that nobody operates' when only one builder is active; Graham agrees he is in that position. — Cost/value concern raised by vendor's hypothetical, accepted by customer; left open (not resolved, tied to enablement plan).

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Is Enterprise worth it for what you're getting', and right now the honest answer is probably not, because you're getting very little.
evidence.context: Customer questions whether Enterprise tier is worth the cost given minimal usage of its features; vendor agrees it probably is not. — Return-on-investment concern on tier spend; vendor proposed Growth tier, customer's security requirement (SSO) makes Growth unviable, so left open with a six-month option proposed.

claims.text: Budget approval thresholds created friction: Acme's finance gets involved above $25k/year, Fable Media's Imogen Price can sign up to £20k (the proposal is about £21.5k), and Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed can approve under 15,000 while Growth (21,600/year) goes to the COO and finance director. Fable Media also asked for monthly billing or starting with 10 users, which was left to manager approval. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed asked about annual prepay, and the vendor said the discount is meaningful but not a halving. Pinewood's Graham Attwood asked about a six-month discount, and the vendor said no discount, only pro-rata.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year, so — yes, finance gets involved.
evidence.context: Purchases above $25,000 a year trigger finance involvement at the customer. — Budget-approval threshold stated by customer, relevant to deal size and approval path.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
evidence.context: Customer stated her spending authority is capped at twenty thousand; anything above requires founder approval, and the proposed annual cost exceeds that. — Budget constraint; Ben computed the annual figure as twenty-one and a half thousand. Left open.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
evidence.context: Sophie Reed said budget is the biggest risk and that the team may decide it is over-buying and keep Zapier; she also said she can approve tools under 15,000 a year alone, and the Growth price (21,600 a year) goes to the COO and finance director. — Approval threshold and budget risk. Left open; slower process above threshold.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Is there any way to start with ten users? Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
evidence.context: Customer asked whether she could start with ten users or bill monthly to prove the process before committing to an annual contract. — Customer sought lower-commitment pricing; vendor said monthly was 'usually fine' but needed manager approval, so left open and deferred.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: can you confirm the monthly billing thing properly rather than "probably"? Because if that's not actually available I'd rather know now.
evidence.context: Customer wants vendor to confirm monthly billing explicitly, saying she would rather know now if it is unavailable. — Pricing term not confirmed; vendor said he would check with his manager. Deferred.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I could potentially do an annual prepay if that materially changes the number. Does it?
evidence.context: Sophie Reed asked whether an annual prepay would materially change the price; Leo said it gives a meaningful discount but not a halving. Deferred/left open. — Customer probed discount options; vendor said discount is modest.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: Would you discount six months?
evidence.context: Customer asks whether the vendor will discount a six-month term; vendor says no discount and no short-term premium, only pro-rata at the annual rate. — Discount/pricing question on the short renewal option; resolved by vendor offer (no uplift, no penalty).

claims.text: Churned customers cited poor value for money. Oakhill Property's Hazel Wren said they paid £1,800/month for 30 users with 4 logging in, that £19k was not worth it, and that Zapier at about £2,000/year was cheaper. She refused a discount, and said a plan at £500-600/month would have kept them (with approval forms), but no smaller plan exists. Verity Payments' Kwame Boateng and Sarah Lindqvist said the premium was not worth it and the licence cost went unjustified (about $100k/year). Kwame said Workato was only somewhat cheaper, so price was partly but not primarily the reason for switching.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.
evidence.context: Customer says Growth plan at £1,800/month for 30 seats was far more than they needed, since only four people logged in, so they were paying for capacity they never used. — Core pricing/ROI complaint; cost mismatch between seats and actual use. Unresolved: the account is churning.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: nineteen thousand pounds is a member of staff for four months
evidence.context: Customer says the product's value to them is not worth the annual price, and frames the cost as a staff salary. — Main reason for churn; the customer does not dispute product quality. Left open: the vendor did not offer a lower price that changed the decision.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
evidence.context: Customer says the replacement tool, Zapier, costs about £2,000 a year, roughly a tenth of OrbitFlow's price, and they are switching for cost reasons. — Cost comparison behind the churn decision. The customer accepts losing some features for the saving.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: If you can do it for eight thousand now, that tells me you could have done it for eight thousand two years ago, and then I'd be quite cross.
evidence.context: Customer rejected a discount offer from the AE, saying a lower price now would show they had been overcharged earlier. — Vendor (Alastair) offered to look at pricing; customer refused. Resolved by refusal: no discount was agreed, and the customer stayed on the decision to leave.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer and I'd probably have done the compliance one eventually.
evidence.context: Customer says a smaller, cheaper plan would have kept them as a customer, but no such tier exists. — Pricing-structure concern; the vendor confirmed there is no smaller plan and the entry point is Growth. Left open/deferred: the vendor only said it would pass the feedback on.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no, because that's the bit Zapier can't do and it's the only thing I'll actually miss.
evidence.context: Customer says a plan around £500/month would only win them back if it included approval forms, which were the feature they valued most. — Conditional interest in a lower-priced tier; the customer will not buy it without approval forms. Deferred: the vendor said it would pass this on but nothing was committed.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
evidence.context: Customer says the platform was a premium-priced business-user tool that was used as an engineering tool, and that this is not worth the premium. — Open: vendor did not respond to the price point directly; the concern was framed as a value-for-money complaint about the two-year spend.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: And because the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.
evidence.context: Customer says the licence cost was being justified by a business-user autonomy benefit that was not materialising, so the return on investment was lacking. — Open: raised as a reason for leaving; not answered by vendor.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: Couldn't, in the sense that the effort exceeded the value by a factor I couldn't justify to my team.
evidence.context: Customer says the effort exceeded the value by a factor they could not justify to their team, which is the February return-on-investment concern. — Open: this was the trigger for the decision to build a custom integration rather than use the platform; vendor asked for specifics but no pricing response followed.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: one of them costs a hundred thousand a year.
evidence.context: Customer says the platform costs about a hundred thousand a year, and that this cost is hard to justify against the maintenance burden of building in-house. — Open: framed as the price side of the build-versus-buy comparison; the customer did not clearly attribute the figure to Workato.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: Less. Not dramatically less.
evidence.context: Customer says Workato is only somewhat cheaper than OrbitFlow, and that price was partly but not primarily the reason for switching. — Deferred: vendor asked whether it was a price decision and the customer answered that it was partly a price decision at the margin, but not primarily.

claims.text: Some customers said price itself was not the issue: Ember Financial's Noah Williams said the range was as expected, DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel said the headline price would not surprise him, and Harbor Legal's Eleanor Brooks said the Enterprise range does not worry her. Halberd Security's Grace Okonkwo accepted the 7% renewal uplift. Lumen's Fiona Bright had braced for a 15% uplift and found 7% more reasonable.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: The range is roughly where I expected an enterprise workflow product to land. That's not my concern.
evidence.context: Customer said the overall price range was roughly where expected for enterprise, so base price was not a concern; the concern was usage overages. — Customer explicitly deprioritised base price; resolved for base price on the call.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review.
evidence.context: Customer says the headline licence price will not surprise him, but he cares about transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and costs only discovered after architecture review; deferred to proposal transparency commitment. — Pricing concern raised by customer; vendor committed to itemised proposal, so partially addressed but open until the proposal arrives.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: The enterprise range itself doesn't worry me. We buy expensive software.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks says the Enterprise price range is not a concern, but the scope of value is. She will not make a business case that depends on privileged-content use, and she would be less interested if it were upsold. — Price tier is accepted, but the business case must stay within low-risk operational scope. Vendor agreed to scope the proposal that way. Resolved for the Enterprise tier; the privileged-content upsell is ruled out.

evidence.speaker: Grace Okonkwo
evidence.quote: Seven percent on a number that size is not worth an hour of my life.
evidence.context: Grace Okonkwo accepted the 7% standard uplift on renewal without negotiating, saying it was not worth the time to pursue. Resolved: renewal agreed at seven percent. — Renewal uplift; customer dismissed the price increase as too small to contest. Ruth later confirmed 'seven percent, no other changes' in the summary.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Braced for "here's a fifteen percent uplift, sign here."
evidence.context: Customer said she had expected a fifteen percent price uplift at renewal and was braced for it. — Pre-emptive uplift objection; vendor said there is an uplift and would come to it.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: That's more reasonable than I expected.
evidence.context: After hearing the standard uplift is seven percent, customer said it was more reasonable than expected. — Uplift concern largely resolved in the call; the vendor still flagged that the run tier increase is a bigger number.

conflicts.description: Kwame Boateng said price was only partly, not primarily, the reason and Workato was only slightly cheaper, yet Sarah Lindqvist and Kwame also framed the licence cost as unjustified relative to value.
